questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A conventional mortgage is not insured or guaranteed by a federal government agency. This distinguishes it from FHA, VA, and USDA loans. A conventional mortgage is best described as:

answers.text: A loan insured by the Federal Housing Administration
A loan guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs
A residential mortgage loan that is not insured or guaranteed by a federal government agency
A loan funded directly from U.S. Treasury bond proceeds

explanations.a: Wrong — FHA-insured loans are government loans, not conventional.
explanations.b: Wrong — VA-guaranteed loans are government loans, not conventional.
explanations.c: Correct — conventional loans are not backed by any government insurance or guaranty.
explanations.d: Wrong — conventional loans are funded by private lenders, not the Treasury.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Conforming loan limits are established annually by the FHFA and determine which loans Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac may purchase. Higher limits apply in designated high-cost areas. The conforming loan limit:

answers.text: Is set annually by the FHFA based on home-price indices, with a higher limit in high-cost areas and a baseline limit applying to most counties
Is set by HUD each year and applies only to FHA-insured mortgages
Has remained unchanged since 2000 by statutory mandate
Equals exactly 80% of the FHA loan limit in the same area

explanations.a: Correct — FHFA annually adjusts conforming limits per the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008.
explanations.b: Wrong — conforming limits are set by FHFA for Fannie/Freddie, not by HUD for FHA.
explanations.c: Wrong — limits are adjusted annually, not frozen.
explanations.d: Wrong — conforming and FHA limits are set independently by different agencies.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: When a residential loan amount exceeds the applicable conforming limit, it cannot be purchased by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac under standard programs. Lenders hold or securitize such loans through private channels. A jumbo mortgage is:

answers.text: Any loan secured by a multi-unit residential property, regardless of amount
A loan with an interest rate exceeding the prevailing APOR by more than 1 percentage point
A loan secured exclusively by non-owner-occupied investment real estate
A residential mortgage loan in an amount exceeding the applicable FHFA conforming loan limit

explanations.a: Wrong — property type does not define jumbo; loan amount does.
explanations.b: Wrong — rate spread above APOR defines HPML status, not jumbo.
explanations.c: Wrong — occupancy type does not define jumbo; loan amount does.
explanations.d: Correct — any residential loan exceeding the applicable FHFA conforming limit is a jumbo.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Fannie Mae operates in the secondary mortgage market and purchases loans from approved lenders. Its purchase of eligible loans provides liquidity that enables new origination. Fannie Mae's primary function is to:

answers.text: Originate residential mortgage loans directly to consumers through retail branches
Purchase eligible mortgage loans from approved lenders to provide liquidity to the secondary mortgage market
Issue federal mortgage insurance protecting lenders from default losses
Regulate state mortgage licensing requirements through the NMLS

explanations.a: Wrong — Fannie Mae is a secondary-market entity, not an originator.
explanations.b: Correct — Fannie Mae buys eligible conforming mortgages from lenders, providing capital for new lending.
explanations.c: Wrong — FHA provides mortgage insurance; Fannie Mae does not.
explanations.d: Wrong — NMLS licensing is governed by the SAFE Act and state regulators.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Three major entities support the U.S. secondary mortgage market. Only one carries a full U.S. government guaranty on the securities it issues. Ginnie Mae differs from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac in that:

answers.text: Ginnie Mae guarantees MBS backed by government-insured or -guaranteed loans such as FHA and VA, rather than purchasing conventional mortgages
Ginnie Mae is a private corporation while Fannie and Freddie are federal agencies
Ginnie Mae sets the conforming loan limits that Fannie and Freddie must follow
Ginnie Mae purchases conventional conforming loans directly from lenders

explanations.a: Correct — Ginnie Mae is a government agency that guarantees MBS backed by FHA, VA, and USDA loans.
explanations.b: Wrong — Fannie and Freddie are GSEs (not federal agencies); Ginnie Mae is a federal government corporation.
explanations.c: Wrong — FHFA, not Ginnie Mae, sets conforming limits.
explanations.d: Wrong — Ginnie Mae does not purchase loans; it guarantees MBS.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Freddie Mac is the second major GSE alongside Fannie Mae. Both purchase conforming residential mortgages to support secondary-market liquidity. Freddie Mac's primary function is to:

answers.text: Insure mortgages issued by FHA-approved lenders against default
Set maximum LTV guidelines for VA-guaranteed loans
Purchase eligible conventional mortgages from lenders, pool them into MBS, and provide capital to the primary market
Operate HUD programs including FHA mortgage insurance

explanations.a: Wrong — Freddie Mac does not provide mortgage insurance.
explanations.b: Wrong — VA LTV guidelines are set by VA, not Freddie Mac.
explanations.c: Correct — Freddie Mac buys conforming mortgages from lenders and pools them into mortgage-backed securities.
explanations.d: Wrong — HUD/FHA programs are administered by HUD, not Freddie Mac.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Conventional and FHA loans are the most common product types. Choosing between them for a well-qualified borrower involves comparing insurance terms. A primary advantage of a conventional loan over an FHA loan for a qualified borrower is:

answers.text: Conventional loans require no down payment regardless of credit score

PMI on a conventional loan is generally cancellable per the Homeowners Protection Act once LTV conditions are met, while FHA MIP may remain for the life of the loan depending on origination LTV and term
Conventional loans always carry a lower interest rate than FHA loans
Conventional loans have no income limits or geographic restrictions, while FHA does

explanations.a: Wrong — conventional loans typically require a down payment; 0% down is not a standard conventional feature.
explanations.b: Correct — HPA allows PMI cancellation on conventional loans at 80% LTV; FHA MIP cancellation rules are stricter.
explanations.c: Wrong — FHA loans sometimes have competitive rates; no absolute rate advantage exists for conventional.
explanations.d: Wrong — FHA has no income limits; USDA has income limits.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Fannie Mae's HomeReady program targets low-to-moderate income borrowers with flexible qualification features. Income limits and non-traditional income sources distinguish it. HomeReady is:

answers.text: A Freddie Mac program for first-time homebuyers only
A HUD-sponsored grant covering the down payment for eligible buyers
A USDA guaranteed loan for borrowers in rural communities
A Fannie Mae conventional mortgage program that allows 97% LTV, income limits based on area median income, and the use of boarder or ADU rental income to qualify

explanations.a: Wrong — HomeReady is a Fannie Mae product, not Freddie Mac.
explanations.b: Wrong — HomeReady is a mortgage program, not a grant.
explanations.c: Wrong — USDA and HomeReady are distinct programs.
explanations.d: Correct — Fannie Mae HomeReady offers 97% LTV financing with AMI-based income limits and expanded income sources.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: FHA does not lend money; it insures loans made by approved lenders. The insurance fund is financed by borrower premiums. The FHA insurance mechanism works because:

answers.text: Borrower-paid UFMIP and annual MIP flow into the Mutual Mortgage Insurance fund, which reimburses lenders for losses on insured loans that default
FHA borrows from the Treasury each year to pay default claims on a reimbursement basis
FHA and the lender share underwriting risk equally on every insured loan
Lenders receive a federal subsidy grant equal to expected default losses

explanations.a: Correct — premium revenue flows into the MMI fund, which covers default reimbursements.
explanations.b: Wrong — the MMI fund, not Treasury borrowing, covers claims.
explanations.c: Wrong — FHA insures 100%; the lender bears no credit risk once FHA insurance is in place.
explanations.d: Wrong — lenders are reimbursed from the MMI fund, not federal grants.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Only lenders approved by HUD may originate FHA-insured loans. Approval allows the lender to offer FHA programs to borrowers. To originate FHA-insured loans, a lender must be:

answers.text: Licensed by the VA as a VA-approved lender and meet VA net-worth standards
A federally chartered bank or credit union with at least $100 million in assets
Approved by HUD as an FHA-approved mortgagee
A Ginnie Mae-approved issuer exclusively

explanations.a: Wrong — VA approval is for VA loans, not FHA.
explanations.b: Wrong — HUD approval is not restricted to large federally chartered banks.
explanations.c: Correct — 24 CFR Part 202 requires lenders to be approved as FHA-approved mortgagees.
explanations.d: Wrong — Ginnie Mae issuer approval is for MBS issuance, not FHA origination.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: FHA allows lower down payments than conventional loans. The minimum depends on the borrower's credit score. For a borrower with a credit score of 580 or above, the FHA minimum down payment is:

answers.text: 5.0% of the purchase price
3.5% of the purchase price
10.0% of the purchase price
0.0% for any veteran regardless of other programs

explanations.a: Wrong — 5.0% exceeds the FHA minimum for scores of 580+.
explanations.b: Correct — HUD requires at least 3.5% down for borrowers with scores at or above 580.
explanations.c: Wrong — 10.0% is required for scores between 500 and 579, not for 580+.
explanations.d: Wrong — no-down-payment is a VA feature, not standard FHA.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: FHA mortgage insurance has an upfront premium and an annual premium. The upfront amount is typically financed into the loan balance. The FHA upfront mortgage insurance premium (UFMIP) is:

answers.text: Charged as a percentage of the borrower's gross annual income
Always paid in cash at closing and may never be financed into the loan
Set equal to 1% of the property's appraised value regardless of loan amount
A one-time premium expressed as a percentage of the base loan amount that may be financed into the loan

explanations.a: Wrong — UFMIP is based on the loan amount, not income.
explanations.b: Wrong — UFMIP may be financed into the loan amount.
explanations.c: Wrong — UFMIP is based on the base loan amount, not appraised value.
explanations.d: Correct — UFMIP is a one-time percentage of the base loan amount, typically financed.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: FHA annual MIP cancellation depends on the origination LTV and loan term. Rules vary by when the case number was issued. For an FHA loan with a case number issued after June 2013, a 30-year term, and an origination LTV above 90%, annual MIP:

answers.text: Automatically cancels at 78% LTV under the Homeowners Protection Act
May be cancelled at 80% LTV upon a written borrower request
Is required for the life of the loan
Automatically cancels after 5 years of on-time payments

explanations.a: Wrong — HPA governs conventional PMI; FHA MIP follows separate HUD rules.
explanations.b: Wrong — borrower-request cancellation at 80% is the HPA rule for conventional PMI.
explanations.c: Correct — per HUD Mortgagee Letter 2013-04, MIP is required for the life of the loan when origination LTV exceeds 90% on a 30-year loan with case numbers from that era.
explanations.d: Wrong — 5-year auto-cancellation applies only when origination LTV is 90% or below.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: FHA loan limits cap the maximum loan amount eligible for FHA insurance. Limits vary by location and property type. FHA loan limits are:

answers.text: Set annually by HUD for each county and MSA, varying by property type (1-4 units) and geographic area
Set by FHFA to match conforming loan limits in every area
Fixed nationally at a single figure for all counties and property types
Set by individual lenders based on their own risk appetite

explanations.a: Correct — HUD sets FHA limits annually at the county level, varying by unit count and area.
explanations.b: Wrong — FHFA sets conforming limits; HUD sets FHA limits independently.
explanations.c: Wrong — FHA limits vary by county and unit count.
explanations.d: Wrong — FHA limits are federally mandated, not lender-determined.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: FHA permits secondary financing in defined circumstances, often to provide down payment assistance. FHA's secondary financing rules require:

answers.text: That no junior lien be placed on an FHA-insured property under any circumstance
That the secondary financing come only from another VA loan
That the second lien be issued only by a private commercial bank
That secondary financing from eligible sources such as government agencies or nonprofits comply with FHA guidelines including combined LTV and repayment requirements

explanations.a: Wrong — FHA permits junior liens when they meet FHA guidelines.
explanations.b: Wrong — VA secondary financing is not a rule; FHA permits eligible public-agency and nonprofit second liens.
explanations.c: Wrong — FHA does not restrict secondary financing to private banks.
explanations.d: Correct — FHA Handbook 4000.1 permits secondary financing from approved sources that comply with combined LTV and repayment standards.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: FHA's 203(k) program lets borrowers finance both the purchase and renovation of a home in a single loan. The loan amount is based on the after-improved value. The FHA 203(k) program:

answers.text: Finances only new construction of a primary dwelling
Allows the borrower to finance both the purchase price and rehabilitation costs in a single FHA-insured loan based on the projected after-improved value
Is limited to luxury renovations in high-cost metropolitan areas
Is identical in structure and purpose to the USDA Rural Development guaranteed loan

explanations.a: Wrong — 203(k) is for existing properties requiring rehabilitation, not new construction.
explanations.b: Correct — 203(k) combines acquisition and rehabilitation financing into one FHA-insured loan.
explanations.c: Wrong — 203(k) is available to all eligible borrowers and properties meeting FHA guidelines.
explanations.d: Wrong — 203(k) and USDA guaranteed loans are entirely different programs.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: VA loan eligibility is based on military service. Different categories have different service requirements. VA-guaranteed loans are available to:

answers.text: Any U.S. citizen who requests them regardless of military background
Only active-duty servicemembers currently deployed overseas
Eligible veterans, active-duty servicemembers, National Guard and Reserve members who meet service requirements, and qualifying surviving spouses
Only recipients of military honors or distinguished service medals

explanations.a: Wrong — VA loan eligibility is tied to qualifying military service.
explanations.b: Wrong — veterans are also eligible; the program extends beyond active-duty.
explanations.c: Correct — 38 USC Chapter 37 defines VA loan eligibility to include these categories.
explanations.d: Wrong — military awards are not an eligibility criterion.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: The VA Certificate of Eligibility is the document that establishes a borrower's VA entitlement. The lender must verify it before proceeding. A VA Certificate of Eligibility (COE):

answers.text: Is issued by the VA to confirm the borrower's service eligibility and available home loan entitlement
Is prepared by the lender using the borrower's DD-214 without VA involvement
Is identical to a credit approval from the Department of Veterans Affairs
Is required only for first-time VA loan users

explanations.a: Correct — the VA issues COEs documenting eligibility and entitlement.
explanations.b: Wrong — the COE is issued by the VA, not prepared by the lender.
explanations.c: Wrong — the COE confirms service eligibility, not credit approval.
explanations.d: Wrong — COEs are required for every VA loan transaction, not only first-time use.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: One of the most cited advantages of VA-guaranteed loans for eligible borrowers is the absence of monthly mortgage insurance. VA loans do not require monthly MI because:

answers.text: The interest rate on VA loans is fixed below the market rate by statute
VA loans have a maximum LTV of 50% to limit lender risk
Borrowers pay FHA mortgage insurance in lieu of separate VA monthly premiums
The VA guaranty compensates the lender for a portion of default loss, making monthly mortgage insurance unnecessary

explanations.a: Wrong — VA rates are market-based, not set by statute.
explanations.b: Wrong — eligible VA borrowers may finance up to 100%; there is no 50% LTV cap.
explanations.c: Wrong — FHA MIP is for FHA loans; VA loans have no monthly MI.
explanations.d: Correct — the VA partial guaranty on the lender's behalf eliminates the need for monthly mortgage insurance.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: The VA Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan streamlines VA-to-VA refinancing. Underwriting and documentation are minimized. The VA IRRRL generally:

answers.text: Allows cash-out up to the full appraised value of the property
Refinances an existing VA loan into a new VA loan with reduced documentation, typically without a new appraisal or credit underwriting, and must result in a lower interest rate or a shorter term
Converts a conventional loan into a VA loan with full VA benefits
Requires full income verification and a new full appraisal in all cases

explanations.a: Wrong — cash-out is not permitted on an IRRRL; the VA Cash-Out program handles cash-out.
explanations.b: Correct — the IRRRL is a streamline VA-to-VA refinance with minimal documentation.
explanations.c: Wrong — the IRRRL cannot convert a conventional loan to VA.
explanations.d: Wrong — a key feature of the IRRRL is reduced documentation; full income and appraisal are not required.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: VA loans charge a one-time funding fee that supports the VA guaranty program. The fee may be financed into the loan. The VA funding fee:

answers.text: Is a one-time charge supporting the VA guaranty program that may be financed into the loan and varies based on loan type, down payment, and prior VA loan use
Is a monthly fee equal to 0.5% of the remaining loan balance
Is charged only to subsequent VA users and never to first-time borrowers
Is structurally identical to the FHA upfront MIP

explanations.a: Correct — the VA funding fee is one-time, financeable, and varies by down payment and prior use.
explanations.b: Wrong — the funding fee is one-time, not monthly.
explanations.c: Wrong — first-time VA borrowers also pay the funding fee (unless exempt).
explanations.d: Wrong — the VA funding fee differs in structure and purpose from FHA UFMIP.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: USDA Rural Development guaranteed loans support homeownership in rural communities. Property location is a qualifying factor. USDA-guaranteed loans require the property to be:

answers.text: Located in any county with a total population under 1 million people
Located within 50 miles of a metropolitan statistical area boundary
Located in an area designated as rural or eligible under USDA's online eligibility maps
Located in a Qualified Opportunity Zone designated by the IRS

explanations.a: Wrong — USDA eligibility is map-based, not tied to a raw population floor.
explanations.b: Wrong — distance from an MSA boundary is not the USDA test.
explanations.c: Correct — USDA defines eligible areas on an online property eligibility map.
explanations.d: Wrong — QOZ designation is a Treasury/IRS tax-incentive concept, not a USDA loan requirement.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: USDA guaranteed loans also have income eligibility requirements to focus benefits on moderate-income borrowers. Household income is the measure. USDA guaranteed loans require:

answers.text: The borrower to have no current income and be receiving public assistance
Household income to be at or below 115% of the area median income for the household size in the eligible area
The borrower to be a first-time homebuyer in all cases
The borrower to be at least 62 years of age

explanations.a: Wrong — USDA targets moderate-income households, not zero-income.
explanations.b: Correct — USDA sets household income eligibility at 115% of AMI.
explanations.c: Wrong — first-time homebuyer status is not required.
explanations.d: Wrong — there is no age requirement for USDA guaranteed loans.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: USDA guaranteed loans use an upfront guarantee fee and an annual fee rather than PMI. These fees fund the program's guarantee reserves. USDA guarantee fees are:

answers.text: Set equal to FHA's upfront MIP and annual MIP amounts
Required only on USDA direct loans, not guaranteed loans
Waived for all first-time homebuyers in eligible areas
An upfront guarantee fee that may be financed into the loan and an annual fee paid monthly, both set by USDA regulation

explanations.a: Wrong — USDA and FHA fees are set independently.
explanations.b: Wrong — guarantee fees apply to USDA guaranteed loans, not only direct loans.
explanations.c: Wrong — USDA does not universally waive fees for first-time buyers.
explanations.d: Correct — USDA charges an upfront guarantee fee plus an annual fee, both established by regulation.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: The Home Equity Conversion Mortgage is the FHA-insured reverse mortgage available to older homeowners. It converts equity to funds without requiring monthly P&I payments. To obtain an HECM, the youngest borrower must be at least:

answers.text: 55 years old
65 years old
62 years old
70 years old

explanations.a: Wrong — 55 is below the federal HECM age threshold.
explanations.b: Wrong — 65 exceeds the minimum; the HECM threshold is 62.
explanations.c: Correct — 12 CFR 1026.33 and FHA HECM rules require the youngest borrower to be at least 62.
explanations.d: Wrong — 70 exceeds the minimum age threshold.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: HECM borrowers may choose from several disbursement plans. The choice affects how and when proceeds are received. HECM disbursement options include:

answers.text: Lump sum, term payments, tenure payments, line of credit, or a combination of these
A single lump sum disbursement only
Monthly payments from the borrower to the lender to build equity
Automatic reinvestment into the property with no cash to the borrower

explanations.a: Correct — HUD allows lump sum, term, tenure, line of credit, and combination plans for HECM.
explanations.b: Wrong — lump sum is one option, not the only option.
explanations.c: Wrong — that describes a conventional mortgage, not a reverse mortgage.
explanations.d: Wrong — proceeds flow to the borrower, not into reinvestment.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Although HECM borrowers do not make monthly P&I payments, ongoing obligations remain. Failure to meet them may trigger default and foreclosure. An HECM borrower must:

answers.text: Make annual principal payments to prevent the balance from growing
Vacate the property once the loan balance reaches 50% of the original value
Refinance into a conventional mortgage every 10 years to reset the balance
Pay property taxes, maintain homeowners insurance, maintain the property in good repair, and continue to occupy it as a principal residence

explanations.a: Wrong — HECM borrowers do not make any required principal payments.
explanations.b: Wrong — there is no mandatory vacation requirement at any LTV level.
explanations.c: Wrong — no mandatory refinance requirement exists for HECM borrowers.
explanations.d: Correct — these are the borrower's obligations that, if unmet, can result in an HECM default.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Before an HECM may be originated, the borrower must receive independent counseling. The counseling is mandatory and must be documented. HECM counseling:

answers.text: Is optional for borrowers who have a licensed financial advisor
Is required from a HUD-approved counselor before any non-refundable fees are charged or the application is taken
May be waived by the lender for borrowers who have held a prior HECM
Is provided by the originating MLO as part of the loan application process

explanations.a: Wrong — financial advisors do not substitute for HUD-approved counselors.
explanations.b: Correct — 12 CFR 1026.33 and HUD require HECM counseling before any non-refundable fees.
explanations.c: Wrong — counseling is required for every HECM and cannot be waived.
explanations.d: Wrong — HECM counseling must be provided by an independent HUD-approved counselor, not the MLO.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: HECM repayment is triggered by specific life or property events. The loan is typically repaid from home-sale proceeds. An HECM becomes due and payable when:

answers.text: The last surviving borrower dies, sells the property, moves out, or fails to meet borrower obligations such as maintaining taxes and insurance
The loan balance reaches 80% of the original appraised value
The youngest borrower turns 80 years of age
Ten years elapse from the date of origination

explanations.a: Correct — HECMs are due and payable upon death, sale, vacancy, or failure to meet obligations.
explanations.b: Wrong — there is no automatic due-and-payable at 80% LTV.
explanations.c: Wrong — reaching a specific age does not trigger repayment.
explanations.d: Wrong — there is no 10-year trigger.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Adjustable-rate mortgages have an interest rate that changes periodically based on a benchmark. The rate structure is fully defined at origination. The primary components of an ARM include:

answers.text: A fixed rate for the entire amortization term with no adjustments
A balloon payment at the end of 5 years with no rate change before maturity
An index, a margin, an initial fixed period, an adjustment frequency, and periodic and lifetime rate caps
A convertible option that automatically becomes a fixed rate after 10 years

explanations.a: Wrong — a fixed rate for the entire term describes a fixed-rate mortgage, not an ARM.
explanations.b: Wrong — a balloon mortgage has a different structure from an ARM.
explanations.c: Correct — these are the defining components of an adjustable-rate mortgage.
explanations.d: Wrong — a convertible feature is optional and not a core component.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: ARM indices are tied to market benchmarks that reflect short-term rates. LIBOR was phased out after benchmark manipulation concerns. The index now commonly used for U.S. residential ARMs following the LIBOR transition is:

answers.text: The 30-year fixed-rate survey index published by Freddie Mac
The Federal Reserve's published discount rate
The FNMA primary market survey yield
The Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR)

explanations.a: Wrong — the 30-year fixed rate does not serve as an ARM index.
explanations.b: Wrong — the discount rate is not the replacement for LIBOR in ARM products.
explanations.c: Wrong — FNMA primary market yield is not the standard replacement index.
explanations.d: Correct — SOFR is the ARRC-recommended replacement for LIBOR in most U.S. ARM products.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: On an ARM, the margin is a fixed spread added to the index to produce the fully indexed rate. The margin remains constant throughout the loan's life. The margin on an ARM is:

answers.text: The maximum rate increase allowed at any single adjustment period
A fixed percentage spread above the index that, added to the index, determines the fully indexed interest rate
The introductory discount applied below the fully indexed rate for the initial period
The maximum lifetime rate increase permitted above the initial rate

explanations.a: Wrong — the maximum per-period increase is the periodic cap, not the margin.
explanations.b: Correct — margin + index = fully indexed rate.
explanations.c: Wrong — an initial discount below the fully indexed rate is a teaser rate, not the margin.
explanations.d: Wrong — the maximum lifetime increase is the lifetime cap, not the margin.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: ARMs are commonly described by notation showing the initial fixed period and the subsequent adjustment frequency. The notation supports product comparison. A '7/1 ARM' is:

answers.text: An ARM that adjusts every 7 years for the entire loan term
An ARM with a 1-year fixed period followed by annual adjustments for 7 years
An ARM with an initial fixed-rate period of 7 years that adjusts annually thereafter
An ARM that converts to a 1-year fixed rate after 7 total adjustments

explanations.a: Wrong — a 7/1 ARM adjusts every year after the initial 7-year fixed period.
explanations.b: Wrong — the notation means 7-year fixed first, not 1-year fixed.
explanations.c: Correct — 7/1 ARM means 7-year initial fixed period with 1-year adjustment frequency thereafter.
explanations.d: Wrong — 7/1 describes fixed period and adjustment frequency, not a conversion feature.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: ARM rate caps define limits on rate movement. Cap structures protect borrowers from extreme changes. A 5/1 ARM with a cap structure of 2/2/5 means:

answers.text: The first adjustment is limited to 2 percentage points above the initial rate, subsequent annual adjustments are limited to 2 percentage points, and the rate may never exceed the initial rate plus 5 percentage points over the loan's life
The total interest paid is capped at 5% of the original loan amount
The loan term may not exceed 5 years
The lender may increase the rate 2 times per year up to 5 total lifetime increases

explanations.a: Correct — first cap/periodic cap/lifetime cap = 2/2/5 in the standard notation.
explanations.b: Wrong — caps apply to the rate percentage, not the total interest cost.
explanations.c: Wrong — the term is not affected by the rate cap structure.
explanations.d: Wrong — caps limit the size of each adjustment, not the number of adjustments.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A 5/1 ARM starts at 5.50% with a margin of 2.75% and caps of 2/2/5. At the first adjustment, the index is 4.00%. The fully indexed rate would be 6.75% (4.00% + 2.75%). The rate at the first adjustment is:

answers.text: 4.00% (index only, ignoring the margin)
6.75%, since the fully indexed rate of 6.75% is below the first-adjustment cap ceiling of 7.50% (5.50% + 2.00%)
5.50%, unchanged from the initial rate
10.50%, applying the full 5-point lifetime cap immediately

explanations.a: Wrong — the rate is index plus margin, not index alone.
explanations.c: Wrong — the initial rate stays in effect only during the fixed period.
explanations.d: Wrong — the lifetime cap does not apply at the first adjustment.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Some ARM structures may produce scheduled payments smaller than periodic interest. The unpaid interest is added to the principal. Negative amortization occurs when:

answers.text: The borrower makes additional principal payments above the scheduled amount
The principal balance declines faster than the original schedule
The lender forgives a portion of accrued interest under a loan modification
The scheduled periodic payment falls short of the periodic interest accrued and the unpaid interest is added to the outstanding principal balance

explanations.a: Wrong — extra principal payments reduce the balance faster, the opposite of negative amortization.
explanations.b: Wrong — faster principal reduction is the opposite of negative amortization.
explanations.c: Wrong — forgiveness of interest is a modification term, not the definition of negative amortization.
explanations.d: Correct — negative amortization occurs when payments are insufficient to cover accrued interest and the shortfall capitalizes into the balance.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A fixed-rate mortgage offers payment certainty by keeping the interest rate constant throughout the loan term. Budgeting is simplified because P&I does not change. A fixed-rate mortgage:

answers.text: Maintains the same interest rate for the entire loan term, with predictable principal-and-interest payments on a fully amortizing schedule
Resets the interest rate annually to the prevailing prime rate published by major banks
Has an introductory rate that expires after 3 years and adjusts to market
Includes a balloon payment of the remaining principal balance at year 10

explanations.a: Correct — a fixed-rate mortgage has an unchanging note rate and predictable P&I.
explanations.b: Wrong — annual reset is an ARM feature.
explanations.c: Wrong — an expiring introductory rate is a hybrid ARM feature.
explanations.d: Wrong — a balloon at year 10 is a balloon mortgage feature.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Common fixed-rate terms are 15 and 30 years. The trade-off is between monthly payment size and total interest cost. Compared to a 30-year fixed mortgage on the same principal, a 15-year fixed mortgage:

answers.text: Has a lower monthly payment with the same total interest paid
Has the same monthly payment as the 30-year because the rate differs
Has a higher monthly payment but significantly lower total interest paid over the loan's life
Has a lower monthly payment and lower total interest cost simultaneously

explanations.a: Wrong — a shorter term with a fixed loan amount requires a higher payment, not lower.
explanations.b: Wrong — the payment is not the same; it is higher for the 15-year.
explanations.c: Correct — the 15-year's higher monthly payment pays off principal faster and reduces total interest dramatically.
explanations.d: Wrong — it is not possible to have both a lower payment and lower total interest on a shorter term.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Some borrowers opt for bi-weekly payment schedules to accelerate principal reduction. The schedule produces an effective extra monthly payment each year. A bi-weekly mortgage payment plan typically:

answers.text: Doubles each month's scheduled principal-and-interest payment
Pays half the monthly amount every two weeks, resulting in 26 half-payments per year equivalent to 13 full monthly payments, reducing the term and interest cost
Skips one payment per year to reduce carrying costs for the borrower
Converts the mortgage automatically to a 10-year term

explanations.a: Wrong — bi-weekly pays half-monthly each two weeks, not double-monthly.
explanations.b: Correct — 52 weeks ÷ 2 = 26 half-payments = 13 full equivalents per year, accelerating payoff.
explanations.c: Wrong — skipping payments adds interest; bi-weekly adds payments.
explanations.d: Wrong — bi-weekly plans do not change the contractual term; they shorten effective payoff time.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Different mortgage structures vary in how principal is repaid. The fully amortizing structure is standard for most residential mortgages. A fully amortizing mortgage has scheduled payments that:

answers.text: Pay only interest for the first 10 years, then principal plus interest thereafter
Pay principal only, with interest collected in a balloon at maturity
Are deferred entirely for the first 5 years
Pay both principal and interest each period such that the loan balance reaches zero at the end of the scheduled term

explanations.a: Wrong — that describes a partially amortizing I/O loan, not fully amortizing.
explanations.b: Wrong — that is a reverse of a standard loan structure.
explanations.c: Wrong — deferred payments are a product feature, not fully amortizing.
explanations.d: Correct — fully amortizing means scheduled payments retire the entire principal and interest by the final payment.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: An interest-only loan requires the borrower to pay only accrued interest for a specified initial period. No principal is repaid during the I/O period. During the interest-only period, the borrower's monthly payment:

answers.text: Includes both principal and interest as on a fully amortizing loan
Is zero, with all interest added to principal through negative amortization
Covers only accrued interest, leaving the principal balance unchanged
Declines each month as the rate adjusts downward automatically

explanations.a: Wrong — during I/O, payments exclude principal.
explanations.b: Wrong — optional I/O payments still require paying full interest; not paying interest would be negative amortization.
explanations.c: Correct — I/O payments cover only accrued interest with no principal reduction.
explanations.d: Wrong — I/O loans do not have automatic monthly rate declines.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A balloon mortgage uses regular payments sized on a longer amortization schedule but the unamortized principal is due in a single final payment at maturity. Typical balloon maturities are 5 to 7 years. A balloon mortgage is best described as:

answers.text: A loan with regular periodic payments sized as if amortized over a longer period, but with the entire remaining principal balance due in a single large payment at the loan's maturity date
A graduated-payment mortgage that increases by a fixed percentage each year
A reverse mortgage available to borrowers over the age of 62
An FHA-insured loan with mandatory refinance provisions at year 5

explanations.a: Correct — balloon mortgages have regular payments but require a final large lump-sum repayment of unamortized principal.
explanations.b: Wrong — graduated-payment mortgages have increasing payments but no mandatory balloon.
explanations.c: Wrong — reverse mortgages serve a different purpose and population.
explanations.d: Wrong — FHA QM guidelines generally restrict balloon loans.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A temporary buydown reduces the borrower's effective rate during the early years. The cost is typically paid upfront by the seller or builder. A 2-1 buydown:

answers.text: Permanently reduces the note rate by 2 percentage points for the life of the loan
Adds 2 discount points and waives 1 origination point at closing
Converts the mortgage to an ARM after year 2
Reduces the effective rate by 2 percentage points in year 1 and 1 percentage point in year 2, then reverts to the note rate from year 3 forward

explanations.a: Wrong — a 2-1 buydown is temporary, not a permanent rate reduction.
explanations.b: Wrong — points are a separate concept from a buydown structure.
explanations.c: Wrong — buydowns do not convert loan types.
explanations.d: Correct — a 2-1 buydown subsidizes years 1 and 2, then the full note rate applies from year 3.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A graduated payment mortgage starts with below-market payments that step up annually over a defined period. Early payments may not cover all accrued interest. A GPM typically:

answers.text: Maintains constant payments throughout the entire loan term
Starts with scheduled payments below the fully amortizing payment, steps them up annually over a set period, and may produce negative amortization in early years
Reduces the principal balance faster than a standard amortizing loan
Is available only on investment and vacation properties

explanations.a: Wrong — constant payments describe a standard fixed-rate amortizing loan.
explanations.b: Correct — GPMs start low, step up, and may produce early negative amortization.
explanations.c: Wrong — GPMs amortize more slowly in early years due to low initial payments.
explanations.d: Wrong — GPMs are not restricted to non-owner-occupied properties.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A bridge loan is short-term financing used when a borrower buys a new home before the existing one sells. The existing home's equity serves as collateral. A bridge loan is best described as:

answers.text: Short-term financing secured by the departing or new property that provides funds to close on the new home before the existing property is sold, with repayment from sale proceeds
A 30-year fixed mortgage with no down payment requirement for qualified first-time buyers
A government-insured first-time homebuyer loan under FHA's Section 203(b)
A type of reverse mortgage for homeowners between the ages of 55 and 62

explanations.a: Correct — bridge loans are short-term, interim financing retired when the prior home is sold.
explanations.b: Wrong — bridge loans are short-term; 30-year terms are standard mortgages.
explanations.c: Wrong — FHA 203(b) is a standard purchase program, not a bridge product.
explanations.d: Wrong — reverse mortgages require the borrower to be at least 62 and are not bridge instruments.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A rate-and-term refinance replaces an existing mortgage with a new one at a different rate or term. Cash to the borrower is limited. A rate-and-term refinance:

answers.text: Allows the borrower to take cash equal to 50% of the property's equity
Eliminates the right of rescission on all refinance transactions
Replaces the existing mortgage with a new loan that modifies the interest rate, the term, or both, with cash to the borrower limited to a small allowable amount above closing costs
Requires no new appraisal under any circumstance

explanations.a: Wrong — taking 50% of equity in cash defines a cash-out refinance.
explanations.b: Wrong — the right of rescission applies to refinances on a principal dwelling; it is not eliminated.
explanations.c: Correct — rate-and-term refinances change rate or term without significant cash to the borrower.
explanations.d: Wrong — appraisals may be required depending on loan type, program, and LTV.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A cash-out refinance pays off existing liens with a new, larger loan and gives the borrower the difference. LTV and seasoning limits apply. A cash-out refinance differs from a rate-and-term refinance in that:

answers.text: Cash-out applies only to investment properties, not primary residences
A cash-out refinance increases the loan amount beyond what is needed to pay off existing liens, with the excess funds disbursed to the borrower at closing subject to LTV limits
Cash-out refinances have no LTV restriction on any property type
FHA prohibits cash-out refinances on its insured loans

explanations.a: Wrong — cash-out is available on primary, secondary, and investment properties.
explanations.b: Correct — cash-out involves a loan amount above the payoff plus costs, with proceeds to the borrower.
explanations.c: Wrong — LTV limits on cash-out are stricter than on rate-and-term.
explanations.d: Wrong — FHA has a cash-out program, subject to FHA guidelines.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: On conventional owner-occupied 1-unit properties, GSE guidelines apply a maximum LTV for cash-out refinances. This limit is more restrictive than purchase or rate-and-term limits. The typical maximum LTV for a conventional cash-out refinance on a primary 1-unit property is:

answers.text: 95% LTV
90% LTV
100% LTV
80% LTV

explanations.a: Wrong — 95% LTV is a purchase or rate-and-term limit for some programs.
explanations.b: Wrong — 90% is not the standard conventional cash-out ceiling for primary residences.
explanations.c: Wrong — 100% LTV is not permitted for conventional cash-out.
explanations.d: Correct — Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guidelines set the conventional cash-out LTV maximum at 80% for a primary 1-unit property.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: The VA IRRRL streamlines refinancing for existing VA borrowers. Documentation and underwriting are minimized relative to a standard VA purchase or cash-out loan. The VA IRRRL generally requires:

answers.text: That the new loan result in a lower interest rate or a shorter loan term, and that the lender certify the net tangible benefit to the borrower
That the borrower provide two years of tax returns and a new full appraisal
That the loan be converted from a VA loan to a conventional loan
That any existing liens other than the VA loan be paid off at closing

explanations.a: Correct — the IRRRL must produce a net tangible benefit; rate reduction or term shortening is required.
explanations.b: Wrong — the IRRRL is a streamline; reduced documentation is a key feature.
explanations.c: Wrong — IRRRL is VA-to-VA; it cannot convert to conventional.
explanations.d: Wrong — the IRRRL payoff requirement applies only to the existing VA loan.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: FHA streamline refinances reduce documentation for existing FHA borrowers. A net tangible benefit ensures the refinance benefits the borrower. The FHA streamline refinance:

answers.text: Requires a new full appraisal in all cases
Allows the borrower to take cash out up to 100% of the property value
Refinances an existing FHA loan into a new FHA loan with reduced documentation, generally no new appraisal, and a demonstrated net tangible benefit such as a lower monthly payment
Converts an FHA loan into a conventional loan without MI

explanations.a: Wrong — a key streamline benefit is that a new full appraisal is not required in most cases.
explanations.b: Wrong — streamline is not a cash-out program.
explanations.c: Correct — the FHA streamline is a reduced-documentation FHA-to-FHA refinance with a net-tangible-benefit requirement.
explanations.d: Wrong — streamline does not change the loan type from FHA to conventional.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A construction-only loan finances building a new home. The borrower must repay or refinance the loan when construction is complete. A construction-only loan:

answers.text: Carries a standard 30-year term and a fixed rate like a purchase mortgage
Is insured by FHA for the duration of the construction period
Converts automatically to a permanent mortgage upon certificate of occupancy
Covers construction costs during building with a short-term loan that must be repaid or replaced by permanent financing once construction is complete

explanations.a: Wrong — construction-only loans are short-term, not 30-year.
explanations.b: Wrong — FHA insurance for construction requires a specific program; it is not automatic.
explanations.c: Wrong — construction-only loans do not automatically convert; the borrower must separately obtain permanent financing.
explanations.d: Correct — a construction-only loan is temporary and must be paid off or refinanced when building is done.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A construction-to-permanent loan combines construction and long-term financing. A single closing reduces transaction costs. A single-close construction-to-permanent loan:

answers.text: Requires two separate closings and two full sets of closing costs
Funds the construction with interim draws and automatically converts to a permanent amortizing mortgage at completion, with only one closing
Requires an FHA guarantee for the construction phase regardless of program type
Is identical in structure and operation to a standard home equity line of credit

explanations.a: Wrong — single-close means one closing, not two.
explanations.b: Correct — the single-close C2P has one closing, interim draw funding, and automatic conversion.
explanations.c: Wrong — FHA guarantee is required only on FHA C2P programs.
explanations.d: Wrong — a HELOC is an open-end revolving product; a C2P is a mortgage.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: During a construction loan, funds are disbursed in stages based on building progress. Inspections protect the lender and ensure funds match completed work. Construction loan draws are typically:

answers.text: Disbursed in a single lump sum at the start of construction
Disbursed on a fixed monthly schedule regardless of construction progress
Released in stages upon inspection and verification that defined phases of construction have been completed
Disbursed only after a certificate of occupancy is issued for the entire project

explanations.a: Wrong — lump-sum disbursement at the start would leave the lender exposed with no completed work.
explanations.b: Wrong — draw timing is tied to completion milestones, not a fixed calendar.
explanations.c: Correct — draw-based disbursement aligned with inspection-verified construction phases protects the lender.
explanations.d: Wrong — disbursing only at occupancy would leave the builder with no working capital during construction.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Closed-end loans disburse the full amount at closing and are repaid per a fixed schedule. They are the standard mortgage structure. A closed-end mortgage:

answers.text: Disburses loan proceeds in a lump sum at closing and is repaid according to a fixed schedule, with the borrower unable to re-borrow repaid amounts
Allows the borrower to draw and repay funds repeatedly up to a maximum credit limit
Requires interest-only payments for the life of the loan with a balloon at maturity
Is always structured as an open-end revolving line of credit

explanations.a: Correct — closed-end loans are lump-sum disbursed and repaid per schedule; no re-borrowing is permitted.
explanations.b: Wrong — revolving access to repaid funds is a HELOC/open-end feature.
explanations.c: Wrong — I/O with balloon is a distinct product structure.
explanations.d: Wrong — a closed-end loan is by definition not an open-end revolving line.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A home equity line of credit is an open-end credit product secured by the borrower's home equity. The borrower may draw and repay repeatedly up to the credit limit. A HELOC is:

answers.text: A closed-end loan with a fixed lump-sum disbursement at closing
An open-end line of credit secured by home equity with a draw period for repeated borrowing and repayment, followed by a repayment period
An FHA-insured program for first-time homebuyers with a credit limit based on income
A reverse mortgage alternative for homeowners who are 62 and older

explanations.a: Wrong — fixed lump-sum disbursement describes a closed-end HELOAN.
explanations.b: Correct — HELOCs are open-end revolving credit products secured by home equity.
explanations.c: Wrong — HELOCs are not FHA-insured products.
explanations.d: Wrong — HELOCs are available to homeowners of any age who have qualifying equity.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A HELOC and a closed-end second mortgage (HELOAN) are both secured by home equity but have different structures. Choosing between them depends on the borrower's needs. A home equity loan (HELOAN) differs from a HELOC in that:

answers.text: A HELOAN is open-end and revolving while a HELOC is closed-end and fixed
A HELOAN is FHA-insured while a HELOC is not
A HELOAN always carries a variable rate while a HELOC usually has a fixed rate
A HELOAN disburses a fixed lump sum at closing with a set repayment schedule, while a HELOC allows revolving draws up to a credit limit

explanations.a: Wrong — HELOAN is closed-end; HELOC is open-end — the opposite.
explanations.b: Wrong — HELOANs are typically conventional products, not FHA-insured.
explanations.c: Wrong — HELOANs often carry fixed rates; HELOCs often carry variable rates.
explanations.d: Correct — HELOAN is a fixed disbursement closed-end loan; HELOC is a revolving line.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: A HELOC has two distinct phases. The borrower accesses funds during the draw phase and pays down the balance during the repayment phase. The draw phase of a typical HELOC:

answers.text: Requires full principal-and-interest payments from the very first draw
Lasts exactly 5 years for all HELOCs by federal regulation
Allows the borrower to draw up to the credit limit and generally requires minimum interest-only or low monthly payments, after which the repayment phase begins with amortizing payments
Automatically converts to a closed-end fixed-rate loan at the end of the draw period

explanations.a: Wrong — HELOC draw-period payments are typically interest-only or low minimums, not full P&I.
explanations.b: Wrong — draw periods vary by lender and are often 10 years; there is no federal 5-year mandate.
explanations.c: Correct — the draw phase allows revolving access with low payments; the repayment phase requires amortizing payments.
explanations.d: Wrong — conversion to a closed-end fixed-rate product is one option but not automatic or universal.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Amortization describes how a loan is paid off over time through regular payments covering both principal and interest. The process results in a zero balance at the end of the scheduled term. Amortization is best defined as:

answers.text: The gradual reduction of a loan balance through scheduled periodic payments that cover both principal and interest
The increase in a loan balance that occurs when payments fall below periodic interest accrual
An appraisal adjustment applied to account for property improvements since origination
A lender's calculation of the borrower's debt-to-income ratio at underwriting

explanations.a: Correct — amortization is the systematic repayment of principal and interest over the loan term.
explanations.b: Wrong — that describes negative amortization, not standard amortization.
explanations.c: Wrong — appraisal adjustments have nothing to do with amortization.
explanations.d: Wrong — DTI calculation is an underwriting function, not amortization.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Discount points are an upfront fee equal to 1% of the loan amount paid to reduce the interest rate. Each point typically purchases a fractional rate reduction. Paying discount points:

answers.text: Increases the loan's interest rate in exchange for a lower origination fee
Reduces the loan's interest rate for the life of the loan, with each point typically purchasing a rate reduction whose size depends on current market conditions
Is required by Regulation Z on all fixed-rate residential mortgages
Converts a conventional mortgage into an FHA-insured loan

explanations.a: Wrong — discount points lower the rate; they do not raise it.
explanations.b: Correct — discount points are a prepaid interest cost that buys down the rate for the loan's life.
explanations.c: Wrong — paying discount points is optional and not required by Regulation Z.
explanations.d: Wrong — discount points are a pricing tool, not a loan-type conversion.

questions.name: General Mortgage Knowledge
questions.text: Many lenders require borrowers to fund an escrow account so that property charges are paid on time. The servicer manages the account. A mortgage escrow (impound) account:

answers.text: Holds funds that the borrower may withdraw for home repairs and maintenance
Is a savings account held by the borrower at a local depository institution
Replaces the borrower's obligation to maintain hazard insurance
Is an account maintained by the servicer that collects monthly installments from the borrower for property taxes, homeowners insurance, and other property charges, and disburses those funds when due

explanations.a: Wrong — escrow funds are for taxes and insurance, not discretionary withdrawals.
explanations.b: Wrong — the servicer, not the borrower, holds the escrow account.
explanations.c: Wrong — escrow accounts collect insurance premiums but do not replace the borrower's obligation to maintain coverage.
explanations.d: Correct — escrow accounts are servicer-held accounts that collect and disburse property-charge installments.
